title: Every best gift (James 1:17)
hookLine: every good gift comes from the Father of lights

cards: A sundial works only because the light keeps moving. Morning shadows stretch long to the west, shrink to almost nothing at noon, and swing around to the east by evening.
The sun is faithful, but it never holds still, and everything it touches casts a shadow that turns. Winter days are short, summer days are long, clouds come and go.
In the first chapter of a new letter, the letter of James, James looks up at that moving sky and says something about the one who made it.

teach.h: WHICH JAMES? THE LETTER DOESN'T SAY.
teach.b: The letter opens simply: James, the servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad. Which James? The letter doesn't say.
Early tradition named James of Jerusalem, called the brother of the Lord, and Catholic tradition has often identified him with James the Less, one of the twelve. Scholars still discuss it.
Then, almost at once, James talks about trials and temptation, and draws a firm line. When someone is tempted, they shouldn't say God is tempting them.
God tempts no one. Temptation grows from a person's own desires. So where does God come in?
Here, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration."
Some readers hear the lights of Genesis one here: the sun, the moon, the stars, which God made. Those lights move. They wax and wane, rise and set, and the shadows they cast turn all day long.
With him, James says, there's no shadow of alteration. The good he gives isn't a passing mood that will swing around by evening.

teach.h: EVERY BEST GIFT IS FROM ABOVE.
teach.b: And the very next verse names one gift in particular: of his own will God has brought us to birth by the word of truth. Put it together and the line becomes a habit of attention.
The good things in a life, the friend, the meal, the recovery, the morning, have a source, and James traces them up.

how: Catholics give thanks for God's gifts in grace before meals, in the thanksgiving after Communion, and in the Mass itself, whose name Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

games.q: you're facing a hard temptation, and part of you wants to say God put it in your path. what does James say?
o: God is testing you on purpose.
no one should say God tempts them; it grows from our own desires.
it's the stars and the seasons.
games.why: James draws the line firmly: God tempts no one. then he turns it around. what comes from God is every best gift.

practice: Notice where the light is falling right now, near a window if you can.

Then choose one good thing from the past day, something specific, a conversation, a warm meal, a body that carried you around, and trace it up, step by step: who made it possible, and who made them possible.
If you pray, thank God for it, the way James traces it back to the Father of lights; if not, just let yourself be grateful.
